tips.title: Tourist tips
tips.tagline: Getting around, paying, tipping and staying comfortable in New York.

subway.title: Subway and OMNY
items: Tap a contactless card, phone or watch on the OMNY reader at the turnstile or on the bus. No MetroCard needed.
Use the same card or device every time: after 12 paid rides in a 7-day window, the rest of that week's rides are free.
Transfers between subway and bus within two hours are free when you tap the same card.
Uptown means north, downtown means south. Check the sign on the platform or entrance before you swipe in.
Local trains stop at every station; express trains skip some. The sign on the front and side of the train says which it is.
The subway runs 24/7, but nights and weekends often have service changes. Check before you go.

tipping.title: Tipping and tax
items: Sit-down restaurants: 18 to 22 percent of the pre-tax bill is standard.
Bars: about $1 to $2 per drink, or about 20 percent on a tab.
Counter service and coffee: tipping is optional; a dollar or two is appreciated.
Taxis and rideshares: 15 to 20 percent.
Listed prices usually exclude sales tax, which is added at the register (8.875 percent in New York City).

safety.title: Safety and etiquette
items: Let riders off the train before you board, and do not lean on the doors.
On escalators, stand on the right and walk on the left.
Keep bags zipped and phones in hand, not in back pockets, in crowds.
An empty car on a busy train usually has a reason. Pick another car.
Emergencies: call 911. City services and non-emergency questions: call 311.

airports.title: Getting here from the airports
items: From JFK: ride the AirTrain to Jamaica (E, J and Z trains, or the LIRR) or to Howard Beach (A train). The AirTrain fare is paid when you exit.
From LaGuardia: the Q70 LaGuardia Link bus runs to the subway at Jackson Heights–Roosevelt Avenue and to the LIRR at Woodside.
From Newark: AirTrain Newark connects to Newark Liberty International Airport Station, with NJ Transit and Amtrak trains to New York Penn Station.
Yellow taxis charge a flat fare between JFK and Manhattan, plus tolls and tip. Check the current amount before you ride.
Take taxis only from the official lines outside arrivals, and ignore anyone inside the terminal offering a ride.

blurbs.financial-district: Wall Street, the 9/11 Memorial and ferries from the harbor's edge, where the city began.
blurbs.chinatown: Dim sum parlors, bakeries and produce stands packed into narrow downtown streets.
blurbs.lower-east-side: Old tenement blocks, classic delis and a late-night bar scene.
blurbs.soho: Cast-iron buildings, cobblestones and flagship shopping.
blurbs.east-village: Noodle bars, cocktail dens and St. Marks Place energy, open late.
blurbs.west-village: Crooked tree-lined streets, jazz clubs and a slice on every corner.
blurbs.union-square: A busy crossroads with a greenmarket, bookstores and subway lines in every direction.
blurbs.meatpacking-district: Old warehouses turned boutiques, the south end of the High Line and the Hudson waterfront.
blurbs.chelsea: Galleries, Chelsea Market and the High Line overhead.
blurbs.nomad: Grand old hotels, rooftop bars and Madison Square Park next door.
blurbs.koreatown: A block of 32nd Street packed with barbecue, karaoke and late-night soup.
blurbs.midtown: Times Square, Broadway theaters and the skyscrapers you have seen in movies.
blurbs.midtown-east: Grand Central, the Chrysler Building and the tram to Roosevelt Island.
blurbs.upper-west-side: Museums, brownstones and two parks: Central on one side, Riverside on the other.
blurbs.upper-east-side: Museum Mile along Fifth Avenue and quiet townhouse blocks.
blurbs.harlem: Soul food, jazz history and the Apollo on 125th Street.
blurbs.williamsburg: Waterfront parks, rooftop bars, coffee roasters and weekend food markets.
blurbs.greenpoint: Polish bakeries, vintage shops and quiet streets along the East River.
blurbs.dumbo: Cobblestones between two bridges, and the most photographed view in Brooklyn.
blurbs.brooklyn-heights: Brownstone streets above the harbor and a promenade facing Lower Manhattan.
blurbs.park-slope: Brownstones, family cafés and the edge of Prospect Park.
blurbs.bushwick: Warehouse murals, galleries and late-night bars.
blurbs.sunset-park: Brooklyn's Chinatown, taquerias, and a hilltop park looking out over the harbor.
blurbs.flushing: One of the city's biggest Chinatowns: dumplings, food courts and bubble tea.
blurbs.astoria: Greek tavernas, beer gardens and the Museum of the Moving Image.
blurbs.jackson-heights: South Asian and Latin American food along Roosevelt Avenue and 74th Street.
blurbs.long-island-city: Riverfront parks with the best Midtown skyline views, plus MoMA PS1.
blurbs.belmont: The Bronx's Little Italy, centered on Arthur Avenue.
blurbs.mott-haven: Historic rowhouses and a growing arts scene in the South Bronx.
blurbs.st-george: The Staten Island Ferry terminal, with harbor views back to Manhattan.
blurbs.greenwich-village: Washington Square, jazz clubs, old coffeehouses and the streets where the folk revival began.
blurbs.prospect-heights: Brownstone blocks between Prospect Park, the Brooklyn Museum and the Botanic Garden.
blurbs.flushing-meadows: The 1964 World's Fair grounds: the Unisphere, museums and wide lawns next to Citi Field.
blurbs.bronx-park: The Bronx Zoo and the New York Botanical Garden, side by side in the woods along the Bronx River.
blurbs.nolita: Small boutiques, cafés and old Italian bakeries on the tree-lined streets north of Little Italy.
blurbs.hells-kitchen: Theater-district restaurants along Ninth Avenue and the Intrepid on the Hudson.
blurbs.washington-heights: Dominican food and music, The Met Cloisters and cliff-top parks above the Hudson.
blurbs.flatbush: Caribbean bakeries, jerk chicken and roti along Flatbush and Church Avenues.
blurbs.woodside: Little Manila's Filipino restaurants and Irish pubs under the 7 train.
blurbs.tribeca: Wide cobbled streets, converted warehouses and some of the city's most celebrated restaurants.
blurbs.noho: Cast-iron lofts, Bond Street's restaurants and a short walk to both Villages.
blurbs.flatiron: The Flatiron Building, Madison Square Park and a dense run of top restaurants.
blurbs.murray-hill: Quiet townhouse blocks near Grand Central, with classic delis and neighborhood bars.
blurbs.fort-greene: Brownstones around Fort Greene Park, Sunday markets and neighborhood bistros.
blurbs.cobble-hill: Leafy brownstone blocks and Atlantic Avenue's Middle Eastern shops and restaurants.
blurbs.carroll-gardens: Old Italian bakeries, front gardens and a busy restaurant strip along Smith Street.
blurbs.gowanus: Old canal-side warehouses turned into bars, music venues and restaurants.
blurbs.bay-ridge: Middle Eastern and Scandinavian food along Third Avenue, with views of the Verrazzano Bridge.
blurbs.governors-island: A car-free island in the harbor with hammocks, bike paths and hills built for the view.
blurbs.coney-island: The boardwalk, the beach, the Wonder Wheel and hot dogs, at the end of the subway line.
blurbs.riverdale: Leafy hills above the Hudson, old estates and the gardens of Wave Hill.

blurbs.little-italy: Red-sauce restaurants, cannoli and string lights along Mulberry Street, home of the Feast of San Gennaro.

blurbs.fordham: Poe Cottage, Fordham University's campus and busy Fordham Road, near the Zoo and the Botanical Garden.

blurbs.red-hook: A waterfront corner of Brooklyn with old warehouses, Statue of Liberty views and some of the city's best barbecue.

blurbs.sheepshead-bay: A south Brooklyn bay lined with fishing boats, seafood counters and the Emmons Avenue waterfront.
blurbs.laurelton: A leafy southeast Queens neighborhood with a large Caribbean community and late-night Jamaican cooking along Merrick Boulevard.
blurbs.jamaica: Southeast Queens' busy downtown around Jamaica Avenue, with King Manor's colonial farmhouse in King Park and the AirTrain to JFK.
blurbs.greenwood-heights: A hilly slice of Brooklyn between Park Slope and Sunset Park, home to the 478 acres of Green-Wood Cemetery.
blurbs.richmond-town: Staten Island's old county seat, preserved as Historic Richmond Town, an open-air museum of houses and shops from past centuries.
blurbs.glen-oaks: A quiet corner of eastern Queens on the Nassau County line, where the Queens County Farm Museum still works its fields.
blurbs.melrose: A South Bronx neighborhood around Courtlandt Avenue, near the Hub at 149th Street, home to the free Bronx Documentary Center.
blurbs.norwood: A residential neighborhood in the north Bronx, home to the Museum of Bronx History in the Valentine-Varian House.

privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.tagline: What NYCrave keeps, what it sends, and what it never collects.

device.title: Kept on your device
items: Saved places and saved days are stored in your browser's local storage. They never leave your device, and clearing your browser data removes them.
Your light or dark mode choice is stored the same way.
If you install NYCrave, the app keeps a copy of your saved places so they open offline.

location.title: Your location
items: Near me asks your browser for your location only when you tap it.
Distances and walking times are worked out on your device. Your location is never sent to NYCrave or stored.

reports.title: Problem reports
items: When you report a problem with a place, we store the place, the kind of problem and any note you write. There is no name or email field.
To stop floods of reports, the server briefly counts reports per network address in memory. It is not saved.

feedback.title: Feedback
items: When you send feedback, we store your rating, the features you picked, anything you write and the site language. There is no name or email field.
To decide when to ask, your browser counts the pages you have seen and remembers when it last asked. That count stays on your device.

services.title: Services the site uses
items: Map tiles come from OpenFreeMap, so your browser requests them from its servers, as with any online map.
Weather forecasts come from Open-Meteo. NYCrave's server asks for the New York forecast; nothing about you is sent.
When Google Places is switched on, place photos and reviews are fetched by NYCrave's server and shown with Google's attribution.

assistant.title: The assistant
items: Ask NYCrave answers from NYCrave's own data on its server. Questions are not stored.
If AI answers are switched on for the site, questions and the conversation so far are sent to Anthropic, which runs the Claude model, to write the answer. Do not share personal details in the chat.

none.title: What NYCrave never does
items: No accounts, no advertising, no analytics and no tracking cookies.
The only cookie is the sign-in cookie for the editors' admin page.

seasons.title: Seasons in New York
seasons.tagline: The dates worth planning a trip around, from Manhattanhenge to the holiday windows.

henge.title: Manhattanhenge
henge.body: Twice a year the setting sun lines up with Manhattan's street grid and glows at the end of the cross streets, framed by skyscrapers on both sides.
henge.whereBody: Stand as far east as you can on a wide cross street with a clear view to New Jersey: 14th, 23rd, 34th, 42nd or 57th Street. Or look down 42nd Street from
henge.note: Dates are estimated from the sun's position and can be a day off. The American Museum of Natural History announces the exact evenings each spring. Arrive 30 minutes before sunset.

cherryBlossoms.name: Cherry blossoms
cherryBlossoms.body: Pink blossoms fill the Brooklyn Botanic Garden's Cherry Esplanade and paths across Central Park. Peak bloom moves with the weather, usually in April.

manhattanhengeMay.name: Manhattanhenge in May
manhattanhengeMay.body: The sunset lines up with the cross streets. Pick a wide street with a view west to New Jersey.

beachSeason.name: Beach season
beachSeason.body: City beaches have lifeguards from Memorial Day weekend to Labor Day. Coney Island and Orchard Beach are a subway ride away.

manhattanhengeJuly.name: Manhattanhenge in July
manhattanhengeJuly.body: The year's second chance to watch the sun set between the skyscrapers.

fourthOfJuly.name: Fourth of July fireworks
fourthOfJuly.body: Macy's fireworks light up the rivers. The viewing spots change each year, so check the announced location and arrive early.

fallFoliage.name: Fall foliage
fallFoliage.body: The parks turn red and gold, usually peaking from late October into November. Central Park's bridges and Fort Tryon Park are classic views.

marathon.name: New York City Marathon
marathon.body: Runners cross all five boroughs on the first Sunday in November and finish in Central Park. Cheer along First Avenue or in Brooklyn.

thanksgivingParade.name: Thanksgiving Day Parade
thanksgivingParade.body: Giant balloons float down Central Park West and Sixth Avenue to Herald Square on Thanksgiving morning. Arrive early for a spot at the curb.

holidayWindows.name: Holiday windows and markets
holidayWindows.body: Department store windows, the Rockefeller Center tree and Bryant Park's winter village light up the city from Thanksgiving into January.

newYearsEve.name: New Year's Eve
newYearsEve.body: The ball drops in Times Square at midnight. Crowds start gathering in the afternoon; many locals watch from a bar or a rooftop instead.

food.title: The New York menu
food.tagline: The foods the city is famous for, what they are, how locals eat them, and where to try each one.

slice.name: The New York slice
slice.body: A wide, thin slice from a big round pie, sold at counters all over the city. Plain cheese is the benchmark; pepperoni is the classic upgrade.
slice.tip: Fold it in half lengthwise and eat it standing up, like everyone else.

pastrami.name: Pastrami on rye
pastrami.body: Brined, smoked and steamed beef, sliced thick and piled high on rye bread with spicy brown mustard. A Jewish deli tradition from the Lower East Side.
pastrami.tip: One sandwich easily feeds two. Add a pickle.

bagel.name: Bagel and lox
bagel.body: Boiled, then baked, so it's chewy inside with a shiny crust. Top it with cream cheese (a schmear), smoked salmon, capers and red onion.
bagel.tip: Get it fresh from the oven; a fresh bagel doesn't need toasting.

halalCart.name: Chicken over rice
halalCart.body: The street-cart classic: chopped chicken or lamb over yellow rice with salad, pita, creamy white sauce and fiery red sauce.
halalCart.tip: Go easy on the red sauce. It's much hotter than it looks.

dumplings.name: Dumplings from everywhere
dumplings.body: Soup dumplings in Flushing, dim sum in Chinatown, pierogi in Greenpoint, khinkali on the Upper East Side and momo in Jackson Heights. There's a dumpling for every tradition.
dumplings.tip: Bite a small hole in a soup dumpling and sip the broth first.

pho.name: Pho
pho.body: Vietnamese beef noodle soup: a clear, long-simmered broth with rice noodles and thin slices of beef, finished with herbs and lime.
pho.tip: Taste the broth before adding sauces; a good pho barely needs them.

ramen.name: Ramen
ramen.body: Japanese noodle soup, from rich pork tonkotsu to lighter bowls, with noodle bars clustered in the East Village and Midtown.
ramen.tip: Slurping is fine: it cools the noodles and it's how the broth is meant to be enjoyed.

tacos.name: Tacos
tacos.body: Corn tortillas with grilled meats, or Tijuana-style birria dipped in its own consomé, from market counters and late-night trucks.
tacos.tip: Order a couple at a time and eat them hot.

koreanBbq.name: Korean barbecue
koreanBbq.body: Marinated beef and pork grilled at your table with a spread of banchan side dishes. Koreatown's 32nd Street is lined with barbecue spots.
koreanBbq.tip: Banchan refills are usually free. If the staff offer to cook the meat, let them.

bubbleTea.name: Bubble tea and matcha
bubbleTea.body: Milk tea with chewy tapioca pearls, brown sugar syrup or a whisked green matcha latte: the city's favorite afternoon pick-me-up.
bubbleTea.tip: Ask for less sugar; most shops let you choose how sweet.

sweets.name: Sweet New York
sweets.body: Dense cheesecake, giant cookies, the croissant-doughnut cronut and swirled babka: New York takes dessert seriously.
sweets.tip: Portions are big. Order one and share.

fold.title: Fold your slice
fold.body: Folding a slice down the middle keeps the tip from flopping and the oil off your shirt.

counter.title: Know where to order
counter.body: At delis, bagel shops and slice counters you order at the counter. Some delis hand you a ticket at the door: keep it, you pay with it on the way out.

bodega.title: Try a bodega breakfast
bodega.body: Corner stores, called bodegas, make a bacon, egg and cheese on a roll to order for a few dollars. It's the city's unofficial breakfast.

walkIns.title: Book, or go early
walkIns.body: Popular restaurants fill up weeks ahead. Many keep bar seats for walk-ins, so arrive right at opening or late in the evening.

cash.title: Carry a little cash
cash.body: Some old-school spots, carts and bakeries are cash only, and small shops may have a card minimum.

late.title: Eat late
late.body: The city stays hungry: slice shops, halal carts and diners serve well past midnight in busy neighborhoods.

walks.title: Walks & hikes
walks.tagline: Forest trails, waterfront paths and a famous bridge in all five boroughs, with how far, how hard and how to get there.
walks.noSubway: No subway nearby: take a bus, or the ferry on Staten Island.
walks.empty: No walks match these filters. Try another borough or level.

inwood.title: Inwood Hill Park
inwood.body: Manhattan's last natural forest. Trails climb through tulip trees, oaks and maples to the top of the hill, with views over the Hudson.
highlights: Two cottonwoods older than the park, at the top of the hill

highbridge.title: Highbridge Park
highbridge.body: Forest trails above the Harlem River beside the High Bridge, the oldest standing bridge in New York City, along the route of the Old Croton Aqueduct.
highlights: The High Bridge, now a footpath to the Bronx
Black cherry and northern oak woods

fortTryon.title: Fort Tryon Park
fortTryon.body: Wooded paths past the city's largest glacial pothole and The Met Cloisters, with views out to the Hudson and the Palisades.

brooklynBridge.title: Brooklyn Bridge
brooklynBridge.body: Walk the raised promenade of the 1883 bridge from City Hall to DUMBO: 6,016 feet with its approaches, the skyline behind you and the harbor below.
highlights: Finish in DUMBO for the classic views

reservoir.title: The Reservoir loop
reservoir.body: The 1.58-mile track around the Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis Reservoir, on soft gravel, with some of Central Park's best skyline views.
highlights: The fountain and the San Remo towers

centralParkLoop.title: Central Park's full loop
centralParkLoop.body: The park drives make a 6.1-mile loop with a lane for runners and walkers, from Columbus Circle around both ends of the park.
highlights: The steepest hills are on the upper loop
Harlem Meer at the north end

prospectWoods.title: Prospect Park woodland trails
prospectWoods.body: Four short trails start by the Audubon Center at the Lincoln Road entrance: the Midwood (0.75 mi), Brooklyn's oldest remaining forest, the Lullwater (1 mi), and the Waterfall and Peninsula (0.5 mi each).
highlights: Fallkill Falls, the first of six waterfalls

saltMarsh.title: Salt Marsh Nature Trail
saltMarsh.body: A 0.8-mile trail from the Salt Marsh Nature Center along the shore toward Jamaica Bay, then through tall grass where rabbits and pheasants hide.
highlights: Starts behind the Salt Marsh Nature Center

vanCortlandt.title: Van Cortlandt Park
vanCortlandt.body: The city's third-largest park: a 2-mile trail through three different forests at the north end, plus wetlands, a lake for birding and remnants of the Old Croton Aqueduct.

pelhamBay.title: Pelham Bay Park
pelhamBay.body: Trails through some of the city's oldest oak trees in its largest park, out to shoreline views, the Twin Islands and the tidal marsh at Turtle Cove.

soundview.title: Soundview Park
soundview.body: An easy 1.75-mile trail where the Bronx River meets the East River, past the amphitheater, a butterfly garden and grasslands.

forestPark.title: Forest Park
forestPark.body: The largest continuous oak forest in Queens, with color-coded trails past kettle ponds: a century-old pine grove on the orange trail and birding at Strack Pond on the red.
highlights: Pine grove on the orange trail
Strack Pond on the red trail

alleyPond.title: Alley Pond Park
alleyPond.body: Trails through oak and hickory forest and glacial kettle ponds, with salt marsh views at the north end by the Environmental Center.

greenbelt.title: Staten Island Greenbelt
greenbelt.body: A 2,800-acre chain of parks in the middle of Staten Island with more than 35 miles of trails through forest and wetland. Start at the Greenbelt Nature Center.

cloveLakes.title: Clove Lakes Park
cloveLakes.body: An easy 3-mile trail past valley lakes, up wooded hills and over old bridges, to New York City's largest tulip tree.

goldenHour.title: Golden hour
goldenHour.tagline: Today's light, minute by minute, and photo walks timed to catch it.
goldenHour.skyBody: Worked out from the sun's position over New York for today's date. The marker shows where the light is right now.
goldenHour.walksIntro: Short walks between photo spots, scheduled for today's sun. Start at the time shown and each stop lands in its best light.
goldenHour.note: Times assume a short stop at each spot. Tall buildings can hide a low sun, so arrive a little early, and check the weather: clouds can make or break the light.

dumboSunrise.title: DUMBO at sunrise
dumboSunrise.body: Catch first light on the Brooklyn Bridge, then the classic Manhattan Bridge frame on Washington Street before the crowds, and finish at the water on Pebble Beach.

centralParkMorning.title: Central Park morning
centralParkMorning.body: Low morning sun over the Pond at Gapstow Bridge, the arcade and fountain of Bethesda Terrace, then Bow Bridge across the Lake.

brooklynSunset.title: Brooklyn sunset
brooklynSunset.body: Watch the sun go down behind Lower Manhattan from the Brooklyn Heights Promenade, then walk to Pebble Beach as the skyline lights up.

midtownBlueHour.title: Midtown blue hour
midtownBlueHour.body: Start on Tudor City Bridge in the last sun, turn to the Chrysler Building as the sky goes blue, and end in the glow of Times Square.

villageNight.title: Village to Chinatown by night
villageNight.body: The Washington Square Arch in golden light, Mulberry Street's string lights at dusk, then the bend of Doyers Street after dark.

fidiSunrise.title: Financial District at sunrise
fidiSunrise.body: Beat the crowds to Fearless Girl facing the Stock Exchange, then the Charging Bull a few steps away, and finish on cobbled Stone Street as the low sun lights the old buildings.

goldenHour.cta: Plan a photo walk timed to today's golden hour

guides.title: Guides
guides.tagline: Everything on NYCrave for a kind of day: free, rainy, with kids, late or romantic.

free.title: Free NYC
free.tagline: Parks, piers, bridges, views and museums that cost nothing.
free.intro: Some of New York's best moments are free: walking a bridge at sunset, a ferry past the Statue of Liberty, a pier at dusk. Every place here is free to enter.
tips: The Staten Island Ferry is free and sails past the Statue of Liberty, around the clock.
Some museums have free or pay-what-you-wish times; check each museum's own site before you go.
Parks and piers keep their own hours, and many close at 1 AM.

rainyDay.title: Rainy day
rainyDay.tagline: Museums, food halls, cafés and shops to wait out the weather.
rainyDay.intro: When it pours, head indoors: big museums take hours, food halls feed everyone, and a good café or bookstore makes a gray afternoon feel planned.
tips: Museums get busier on wet weekends, so go early in the day.
Pay the subway fare by tapping a contactless card or phone at the turnstile (OMNY).
Check a place's hours before you go; the hours on each page come from official sources.

withKids.title: With kids
withKids.tagline: Places that work for families, from museums to carousels and parks.
withKids.intro: Places where kids are welcome and have room to be kids: hands-on museums, parks with space to run, and food everyone will eat.
tips: Up to three children 44 inches (112 cm) tall or shorter ride the subway free with a paying adult.
Not every subway station has an elevator; the MTA's map shows the accessible ones if you have a stroller.
Many museums are free for young children; check each ticket page for the ages.

lateNight.title: Late night
lateNight.tagline: Bars, slices and spots that keep going after dark.
lateNight.intro: New York keeps going after dark. These are the places tagged for late nights, from old saloons to rooftop bars and food that tastes best after midnight.
tips: The subway runs 24 hours a day, though trains come less often late at night.
Kitchens often close before the bar does; check the hours on each page.
Many bars are 21+ and check ID at the door, so bring a photo ID.

dateNight.title: Date night
dateNight.tagline: Candlelit dinners, cocktail bars, views and walks for two.
dateNight.intro: For a night out together: restaurants worth dressing up for, cocktail bars with atmosphere, and views to walk to afterward.
tips: Book popular restaurants ahead, especially Thursday to Saturday.
Pair dinner with a walk: the waterfront and bridges are lit up at night.
Some cocktail bars have dress codes or age limits; check the place's own site.

cheapEats.title: Cheap eats
cheapEats.tagline: Slices, dumplings, bagels and more for a few dollars.
cheapEats.intro: Eating well in New York doesn't have to cost much. These places are tagged as cheap eats or sit at the lowest price level.
tips: Some classic spots are cash only; carry a little cash.
New York sales tax (8.875%) is added at the register, not shown on most menus.
At sit-down restaurants a tip of 18 to 20% is expected; at a counter it's optional.

solo.title: Solo
solo.tagline: Counters, cafés, museums and walks that are easy to enjoy on your own.
solo.intro: New York is one of the easiest cities to explore alone. These places are tagged as good on your own: counter seats, quiet cafés, museums and walks at your own pace.
tips: Sit at the bar or counter: it is often the quickest way to get a seat without a reservation.
Museums, bookstores and cafés are easy places to spend time alone, with no one to keep up with.
At night, stick to busy, well-lit streets and keep your phone charged.

outdoors.title: Outdoors
outdoors.tagline: Parks, piers, gardens, markets and views in the open air.
outdoors.intro: For days when you want sky overhead: parks and piers, gardens, open-air markets, outdoor seating and views. Every place here is tagged as outdoors.
tips: Most city parks follow NYC Parks' standard hours, 6 AM to 1 AM, unless posted otherwise.
Summer days are often hot and humid: bring water and look for shade in the afternoon.
The home page shows today's forecast and rain chance before you head out.

history.title: History
history.tagline: House museums, landmarks and the stories of how New York became New York.
history.intro: Colonial-era houses, a Revolutionary-era tavern, an immigrant tenement and the homes of an inventor and a jazz legend: New York's past is still standing in all five boroughs, often a short subway ride away.
tips: Many house museums open only a few days a week, often in the afternoon. Check the hours on each page before you go.
Some sites are seen on guided tours at set times; book ahead where the site asks you to.
Pair a house museum with a walk around its neighborhood; most are a short walk from the subway.
